problem:
Given a string s, return the length of the longest contiguous substring that contains no repeated characters.

Example: s = "abcabcbb" -> 3 ("abc")
Example: s = "bbbbb" -> 1
Example: s = "pwwkew" -> 3 ("wke")

data.generator_code:
import string

def generate(rng, n):
    chars = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + " !@#$%^&*()"
    s = "".join(rng.choice(chars) for _ in range(n))
    return [s]

def generate_worst(rng, n):
    chars = string.ascii_lowercase[:min(n, 26)]
    s = "".join(rng.choice(chars) for _ in range(n))
    return [s]

data.key_insight: Maintain a window of unique characters using two pointers (left and right). When a duplicate character is encountered at the right pointer, advance the left pointer past the previous occurrence of that character.

steps.title: Initialize pointers and hash map
steps.detail: Create a dictionary to store the most recent index of each visited character. Set both the left pointer of the sliding window and the maximum length variable to zero.

steps.title: Expand the right pointer
steps.detail: Iterate through the string with the right pointer. If the current character is already in the hash map and its last seen index is greater than or equal to the left pointer, update the left pointer to be one position after that last seen index.

steps.title: Update character position and maximum length
steps.detail: Store or update the current character's index in the hash map. Calculate the current window size (right - left + 1) and update the maximum length if this size is larger.

data.space_complexity: O(min(n, m)) where m is the size of the charset

data.pattern_summary: Sliding window is used when dealing with contiguous subarrays or substrings, allowing you to maintain a range of elements (a window) and dynamically adjust its boundaries rather than re-evaluating from scratch.

pattern_options.name: Sliding window
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. We need to find the longest contiguous substring meeting a specific condition, which maps directly to expanding and shrinking a window across the string.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. While two pointers are used to implement the window, this pattern specifically requires managing a contiguous range of elements dynamically, making sliding window the more precise categorization.

pattern_options.name: Dynamic programming
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. Overlapping subproblems do not form the primary structure here; we are searching for a valid contiguous sequence using boundary adjustments.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Incorrect. A hash map might be useful as a helper tool to track character positions, but it does not define the overall algorithmic pattern for processing substrings.

signals.hint: Contiguous sequences processed for a maximum length strongly point toward maintaining a sliding window.
This condition dictates when your window must shrink or reset its left boundary.

data.brute_force_idea: Generate every possible contiguous substring of the input string, check each one to see if it contains any duplicate characters, and keep track of the maximum length found among the valid ones.
data.brute_force_why: There are O(n^2) possible substrings, and checking each substring for uniqueness takes O(n) time due to building a set and measuring its length.
data.bottleneck: Re-checking the entire substring for duplicates from scratch every time using set() and len() repeats work that was partially done in previous iterations.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how many times characters are re-scanned inside substrings that overlap heavily with one another.
When you slide from one substring to the next by adding a single character, do you really need to rebuild the set for all the previous characters?
Think about how you can remember the last seen position of each character so you only adjust boundaries instead of re-examining the whole substring.

events.label: Coach: why the complexity is what it is

data.insight: The brute force approach repeatedly checks overlapping substrings from scratch, leading to redundant work. The sliding window approach maintains a dynamic range [left, right] using a hash map to instantly jump past duplicate characters, ensuring each character in the string is visited at most twice.

derivation.note: The for loop iterates through each character of the string s exactly once.
Dictionary lookup checks if the character exists in constant average time.
The left pointer updates in constant time when a duplicate is found within the window.
Updating the character index in the dictionary takes constant average time.
Calculating the maximum length takes constant time per iteration.

data.time_summary: Line 7 runs n times, and lines 8 through 11 execute in constant time O(1) on each iteration. The measured steps scale linearly with n (n^1.01), confirming a total time complexity of O(n).
data.space_summary: The hash map stores the most recent index of each character within the current window. In the worst case, space complexity is O(min(n, m)), where m is the size of the character set.
data.takeaway: When searching for contiguous subarrays or substrings with unique elements, use a sliding window with a hash map to track positions and adjust the left boundary in O(1) time.
mistakes: Forgetting to check if the duplicate character's recorded index is greater than or equal to the current left boundary.
Failing to update the character's latest index in the map on every iteration.
Confusing substring length calculation by using right - left instead of right - left + 1.

events.label: Tutor: build the visual explanation

data.overview: The sliding window algorithm finds the longest substring without repeating characters by maintaining a window defined by left and right pointers. It expands the right pointer and dynamically jumps the left pointer forward whenever a duplicate character is found.
data.intuition: Imagine looking through a sliding glass window placed over a row of letters. You slide the right edge forward one by one, but the moment you see a duplicate letter inside your window, you slide the left edge up just past the old copy of that letter to keep everything unique.
